skills.name: Measure the volume of liquids, regular and irregular solids

note.text:
Volume is the space an object occupies. SI unit: m³; also cm³ and litres (1 L = 1000 cm³ = 1 dm³; 1 mL = 1 cm³; 1 m³ = 1000 L).
• Liquids: measuring cylinder, burette, pipette. Read at the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level with it.
• Regular solids: calculate (cuboid: l × w × h; cylinder: πr²h).
• Irregular solids: displacement. Volume = (reading with the object) − (reading without it), or use an overflow (eureka) can.

sections.heading: Volume and its units
sections.text:
Volume is the amount of space something takes up. The SI unit is the cubic metre (m³), but for small amounts we use cm³ and litres.
• {1} L = {1000} cm³ = {1} dm³
• {1} mL = {1} cm³
• {1} m³ = {1000} L
A water tank at home may hold {1000} L, which is {1} m³.

sections.heading: Reading a measuring cylinder
sections.text:
Water in a narrow tube curves at the surface: this curve is the meniscus. Read the scale at the bottom of the meniscus, with your eye level with it.
Looking from above or below gives a wrong reading (parallax error).
First work out what each small mark is worth: on a {100} mL cylinder with ten small marks between labels, each mark is {1} mL or {2} mL.

sections.heading: Regular and irregular solids
sections.text:
For a regular shape, measure and calculate: a cuboid is length × width × height.
For an irregular shape like a stone, use displacement. Read the water level, lower the stone in gently on a thread, and read again. The rise in level is the volume of the stone.
For a large stone use an overflow (eureka) can and measure the water that overflows.

key_words.meaning: the space an object takes up
the curved surface of a liquid in a tube
the liquid pushed aside by an object put into it
a wrong reading from looking at a scale from the side

mistake.wrong: Stone: water rises from {40} mL to {52} mL, so the stone is {52} cm³
mistake.why: Only the rise in level is due to the stone.

worked_example.problem: Water in a measuring cylinder reads {b} mL. A stone is lowered in and the level rises to {a} mL. Find the volume of the stone.
steps: The stone pushes aside (displaces) its own volume of water.

cards.idea: Read a measuring cylinder at the bottom of the meniscus, eye level with it.
example: Each small mark is {2} mL on a {100} mL cylinder.

cards.idea: Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height.
Volume of an irregular solid = rise in the water level.
example: {50} mL → {65} mL: the stone is {15} cm³.

check.prompt: What is the volume of the stone (cm³)?

misconceptions.explain: That is the reading with the stone. Subtract the reading before.

solution: Volume of stone = rise in the water level.

questions.prompt: How much water is in the measuring cylinder (mL)?

misconceptions.explain: Read at the bottom of the curved surface, not at the edges.

solution: The bottom of the meniscus is at {answer} mL.

questions.prompt: A wooden block is {l} cm long, {w} cm wide and {h} cm high. Find its volume (cm³).

misconceptions.explain: That is the area of the base. Multiply by the height too.

questions.prompt: What is the volume of the stone (cm³)?

misconceptions.explain: That is the reading with the stone. Subtract the reading before.

solution: Volume of stone = rise in the water level.

questions.prompt: A cylindrical water tank has radius {r} m and height {h} m. Find its volume in litres (π = {3.14}).

misconceptions.explain: That is in m³. Multiply by {1000} for litres.
